clinicalPearls: Plasma cell disorders are monoclonal neoplasms of late B-lymphocyte lineage; the group includes multiple myeloma (MM), Waldenström's macroglobulinemia, primary (AL) amyloidosis, and the heavy chain diseases, also termed monoclonal gammopathies, paraproteinemias, plasma cell dyscrasias, or dysproteinemias (Harrison 22e p.883).

MGUS is vastly more common than myeloma, occurring in ~1% of the population aged >50 and up to ~10% of those aged >75; no specific intervention is indicated and annual (or less frequent) follow-up is adequate, with closer monitoring only for higher-risk MGUS (Harrison 22e p.887-890).
About ~1% of MGUS patients per year progress to myeloma, but essentially all cases of myeloma are preceded by MGUS (Harrison 22e p.887).

Higher-risk MGUS features are non-IgG subtype, abnormal kappa/lambda free light chain ratio, and serum M-protein >15 g/L (1.5 g/dL); absence of all three predicts ~5% progression while presence of all three predicts ~60% progression over 20 years (Harrison 22e p.887).

Diagnostic workup for a monoclonal protein uses serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP) for quantitation and immunoelectrophoresis/immunofixation for confirmation of a single heavy and/or light chain; serum free light chain assay and urine studies (UPEP) detect light-chain-only and Bence Jones disease (Harrison 22e p.883-884).

An M component must be present at ~5 g/L (0.5 g/dL) to be accurately quantitated by electrophoresis; the serum M-protein level is a reliable measure of tumor burden but is not specific enough to screen asymptomatic patients (Harrison 22e p.883-884).

MGUS diagnostic criteria: serum monoclonal protein (non-IgM) <30 g/L, clonal bone marrow plasma cells <10%, and absence of myeloma-defining events or amyloidosis attributable to the plasma cell disorder (Harrison 22e p.888, Table 116-1).

Waldenström's macroglobulinemia (WM) is a malignancy of IgM-secreting lymphoplasmacytoid cells; unlike myeloma it presents with lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly and its major manifestation is hyperviscosity syndrome (Harrison 22e p.893).

A distinct MYD88 L265P somatic mutation is present in >90% of WM patients and the majority of IgM MGUS, and is used as a diagnostic test to discriminate WM from marginal zone lymphoma, IgM-secreting myeloma, and CLL with plasmacytic differentiation (Harrison 22e p.893).

In WM the IgM may have specificity for myelin-associated glycoprotein (MAG); a peripheral neuropathy may precede the neoplasm and about half of these patients are anti-MAG positive (Harrison 22e p.893).

POEMS syndrome = Polyneuropathy, Organomegaly, Endocrinopathy, M-protein, and Skin changes; patients typically have a severe progressive sensorimotor polyneuropathy with sclerotic bone lesions, and polyneuropathy occurs in only ~1.4% of myelomas with POEMS being a rare subset (Harrison 22e p.893).

AL (primary) amyloidosis is a plasma cell disorder most often caused by clonal bone marrow plasma cells secreting a misfolding monoclonal light chain; it can coexist with multiple myeloma, Waldenström's macroglobulinemia, or non-Hodgkin's lymphoma (Harrison 22e ch.117 p.896-897).
Macroglossia and periorbital ('raccoon-eye') ecchymoses are pathognomonic but uncommon signs of AL amyloidosis, each seen in only ~10% of patients (Harrison 22e ch.117 p.897).
harrison.pathophysiology: In normal B-cell maturation, antigen exposure drives differentiation of mature B lymphocytes into antibody-secreting plasma cells; in plasma cell disorders this control is lost, producing a monoclonal expansion that secretes a single (monoclonal) immunoglobulin or fragment (M component). Clinical manifestations arise from neoplastic cell expansion, from the secreted products (intact immunoglobulin, free light/heavy chains, lymphokines), and from the host response. In multiple myeloma, recurrent chromosomal lesions include hyperdiploidy and 14q32 translocations (e.g., t(11;14), t(4;14), t(14;16)), with errors in immunoglobulin switch recombination implicated in early transformation. Waldenström's macroglobulinemia arises from a post-germinal-center IgM-bearing memory B cell, driven by MYD88 L265P (TLR/IL-1R IRAK and NF-kB signaling, plus BTK/HCK signaling) and frequently CXCR4 mutations. In AL amyloidosis, clonal plasma cells produce a monoclonal light chain (lambda predominates) that misfolds into insoluble amyloid fibrils deposited extracellularly in tissues (Harrison 22e p.883-884, 893; ch.117 p.896-897).

Plasma cell leukemia (>2000 circulating plasma cells/uL)
IgM myeloma (lytic lesions, CD138+ plasma cells, t(11;14))
Heavy chain diseases (gamma/Franklin's, alpha/Seligmann's and IPSID, mu)
Marginal zone lymphoma and CLL with plasmacytic differentiation
nonInfectiousMimics: M components in other lymphoid neoplasms (CLL, B- or T-cell lymphomas)
M components in nonlymphoid neoplasms (chronic myeloid leukemia, breast cancer, colon cancer)
Nonneoplastic conditions: cirrhosis, sarcoidosis, parasitic diseases, Gaucher's disease, pyoderma gangrenosum
Autoimmune conditions: rheumatoid arthritis, myasthenia gravis, cold agglutinin disease
Post organ-transplant immunosuppression (and rarely allogeneic transplant)
Skin diseases with monoclonal gammopathy: lichen myxedematosus (papular mucinosis), necrobiotic xanthogranuloma (~10% progress to myeloma)
Mixed cryoglobulinemia (IgM/IgA complexed with IgG) seen in rheumatoid arthritis and other autoimmune disease, usually not associated with malignancy
additionalInvestigations: Serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP) for M-protein quantitation
Serum and urine immunofixation electrophoresis (SIFE/UIFE) to confirm monoclonality and identify heavy/light chain type
Urine protein electrophoresis (UPEP) / 24-h urine for Bence Jones (free light chain) protein
Serum free light chain assay with kappa/lambda ratio (essential to assess ratio, not just absolute level, since renal insufficiency nonspecifically raises both)
Bone marrow biopsy/aspirate for clonal plasma cell percentage and CD138+ / kappa or lambda light chain restriction by flow cytometry, immunohistochemistry, or in situ hybridization
MYD88 (L265P) and CXCR4 mutation testing to discriminate WM from MZL, IgM myeloma, and CLL
Skeletal survey, CT, or PET-CT for osteolytic lesions; MRI of spine/pelvis for focal lesions
Serum calcium, creatinine/creatinine clearance, and hemoglobin (to assess CRAB end-organ damage)
VEGF level and evaluation for Castleman's disease when POEMS is suspected
Tissue biopsy with Congo red staining and mass spectrometry-based typing when amyloidosis is suspected (SPEP/UPEP alone are inadequate screens for AL)
redFlags: Hyperviscosity syndrome in Waldenström's macroglobulinemia / IgM gammopathy: headache, visual disturbance, retinal vein segmentation and dilation, epistaxis, altered consciousness, paresis (most IgM is intravascular and responds to plasmapheresis)
Myeloma-defining end-organ damage (CRAB): hyperCalcemia, Renal insufficiency, Anemia, Bone lytic lesions
Spinal cord compression: new lower-extremity neurologic deficit, severe localized back pain, or loss of bowel/bladder control requiring emergency MRI and radiation/decompression
Acute renal failure from light chain cast nephropathy, especially with dehydration
Cardiac involvement in AL amyloidosis (70-80%) is the leading cause of death; low-voltage ECG with pseudo-infarct pattern and thickened ventricles on echo
MGUS with severe polyneuropathy (consider causal IgM/anti-MAG neuropathy)
harrison.prognosis: MGUS carries a low malignant potential, with ~1% per year progression to myeloma (risk stratified by IgG vs non-IgG subtype, free light chain ratio, and M-protein level: ~5% at 20 years with no risk features vs ~60% with all three). Smoldering myeloma progresses to symptomatic MM in ~25% at 5 years with one risk feature and ~76% with all three high-risk features. Waldenström's macroglobulinemia is often indolent and may not require therapy; median survival is reported as ~50 months, with older age, male sex, general symptoms, and cytopenias defining a high-risk group. AL amyloidosis is often rapidly progressive and fatal if untreated (occurs after age 40); very low dFLC (<50 mg/L) predicts significantly better outcome (Harrison 22e p.887-888, 893-894; ch.117 p.896-898).
pitfalls: Do not equate a monoclonal protein with malignancy: distinguish MGUS (clonal marrow plasma cells <10%, M-protein <30 g/L, no myeloma-defining events/amyloidosis) from multiple myeloma, which requires marrow plasmacytosis and myeloma-defining events / CRAB end-organ damage (Harrison 22e p.887-888).

SPEP/UPEP are useful in myeloma but are NOT adequate screening tests for AL amyloidosis, because the clonal light chain is often insufficient to produce an M-spike; use serum/urine immunofixation and free light chain assay (>90% positive) (Harrison 22e ch.117 p.897).

A monoclonal protein alone is not diagnostic of amyloidosis since MGUS is common in older patients; when MGUS coexists with biopsy-proven amyloidosis, AL type must be ruled out and 'smoldering myeloma' patients should be screened for AL (Harrison 22e ch.117 p.897).

WM does not cause bone lesions or hypercalcemia (unlike myeloma); large IgM paraprotein causes little renal excretion so renal disease is uncommon (~20% excrete light chains)—reserve the diagnosis of IgM myeloma for lytic bone lesions with CD138+ plasma cells and t(11;14) (Harrison 22e p.893).
Suspected cryoglobulin: draw blood into a warm syringe and transport in warm water to avoid errors in quantitation (Harrison 22e p.893).
Rituximab can produce an IgM flare in WM—use plasmapheresis first or initially withhold rituximab in patients with high IgM levels (Harrison 22e p.894).
Pseudohyponatremia and a decreased anion gap can occur in myeloma because the cationic M component retains chloride and displaces serum water (Harrison 22e p.887).
harrison.severityClassification: MGUS vs smoldering (asymptomatic) myeloma vs symptomatic multiple myeloma per IMWG criteria (Harrison Table 116-1). MGUS: non-IgM serum M-protein <30 g/L, clonal marrow plasma cells <10%, no myeloma-defining events/amyloidosis. Smoldering MM: serum M-protein (IgG/IgA) >=30 g/L or urine M-protein >=500 mg/24h and/or clonal marrow plasma cells 10-60%, without myeloma-defining events. Symptomatic MM: clonal plasma cells (or plasmacytoma) plus a myeloma-defining event—CRAB end-organ damage (hyperCalcemia, Renal insufficiency, Anemia, Bone lesions) or a biomarker of malignancy (clonal marrow plasma cells >=60%, involved:uninvolved serum free light chain ratio >=100, or >1 focal MRI lesion). POEMS requires polyneuropathy + monoclonal plasma cell disorder + (sclerotic bone lesions / Castleman's / elevated VEGF) + an additional system feature.
management: Manage MGUS with active surveillance rather than treatment, using periodic serum protein electrophoresis, free light chain ratio and blood counts, with follow-up intensity guided by risk features
Treat Waldenstrom's macroglobulinaemia only when symptomatic (cytopenias, hyperviscosity, bulky or constitutional disease) and observe asymptomatic patients
Use rituximab-based therapy for symptomatic Waldenstrom's, combined with chemoimmunotherapy such as bendamustine or a proteasome inhibitor
Employ a BTK inhibitor such as ibrutinib or zanubrutinib, particularly in MYD88-mutated disease
Treat symptomatic hyperviscosity urgently with plasma exchange, and avoid precipitating a rituximab-induced IgM flare when the paraprotein is high
Provide supportive care with transfusion for symptomatic anaemia and management of associated neuropathy or cryoglobulinaemia
Monitor for progression or transformation to myeloma or an aggressive lymphoma
Refer to haematology for risk stratification and treatment planning
